ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> In feature search mode, participants are often faster when a salient distractor is on the screen, with different groups alternatively interpreting this global speedup as suppression (Gaspelin et al., 2015) or a side effect of inefficient serial search (de Waard & Theeuwes, 2026; Liesefeld & Müller, 2020).

> Usually, participants are required to remain still, maintain central fixation, and respond to briefly presented stimuli with a button press -constraints that are methodologically necessary because eye movements create artifacts in EEG data (Lins et al., 1993), but are ultimately conceptually restrictive.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: An enduring topic of scientific interest since the beginning of cognitive psychological research is visual attention.

This phenomenon describes the process by which certain visual percepts are prioritized for deeper processing in the brain, while others receive reduced processing and thereby exert less influence on perception and behavior.
In our daily lives, visual attention is critical to performance across countless situations-from navigating busy traffic to maintaining focus on a friend in a crowded room.

Therefore, understanding the neural mechanisms that dictate how we select relevant visual information and filter out distractions is central to understanding one of the brain's most fundamental cognitive abilities.

Because these attentional processes unravel rapidly in time and are reflected in dynamic patterns of cortical activity, encephalographic measures (i.e. electro-and magneto-encephalography) have been popular tools for their study.

In 2025, attention researchers from across Europe gathered in Amsterdam for two days of meetings, discussion, and debate on current issues and future avenues in the encephalographic investigation of attention.
This perspective piece distills the ideas and topics that emerged from that meeting into a field guide to contemporary encephalographic research on visual attention.
It provides a snapshot of several active research areas in visual attention, highlights where they are heading, and which questions are likely to shape their future.
We hope that this piece will be especially useful for early career researchers looking to enter the field but unsure about what their next research question should be.
How does the brain cope with the overwhelming amount of information it encounters at every moment?
Since Broadbent's Filter Theory was proposed (Broadbent, 1958), this has remained a central question in attention research.
text.formatted: Since Broadbent's Filter Theory was proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Broadbent, 1958)</ref>, this has remained a central question in attention research.

text.text: Alongside major experimental and theoretical advances (Posner, 1980; Treisman & Gelade, 1980), a landmark advance came from Steven Hillyard and colleagues, who demonstrated that scalp-recorded electrophysiological signals-particularly event-related potentials (ERPs)-could reveal the neural mechanisms underlying attentional selection in both auditory (Hillyard et al., 1973) and visual (Van Voorhis & Hillyard, 1977) domains.
text.formatted: Alongside major experimental and theoretical advances <ref type="bibr" target="#b216">(Posner, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b256">Treisman & Gelade, 1980)</ref>, a landmark advance came from Steven Hillyard and colleagues, who demonstrated that scalp-recorded electrophysiological signals-particularly event-related potentials (ERPs)-could reveal the neural mechanisms underlying attentional selection in both auditory <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Hillyard et al., 1973)</ref> and visual <ref type="bibr" target="#b270">(Van Voorhis & Hillyard, 1977)</ref> domains.

text.text: In the ensuing years, electroencephalography (EEG) has become one of the principal methods for investigating the neural mechanisms of human attention.

Methodological advances have substantially broadened the range of neural signals that can be measured, allowing researchers to pursue increasingly intricate questions about the mechanisms and nature of human attention.

ERPs and oscillatory analyses continue to provide precise, well-validated markers of attention, and they are now complemented by multivariate decoding techniques, as well as the emergence of rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT), which open new avenues for studying attentional operations that were previously only studied via behavior.

Collectively, this research has significantly advanced the understanding of how humans effectively direct attention to a subset of meaningful percepts while filtering those deemed irrelevant or distracting.
In the summer of 2025, attention researchers from across Europe gathered in Amsterdam for an international symposium titled "Advances in the Encephalographic Study of Attention."
During this two-day forum, researchers presented and debated their latest findings and emerging ideas.
This meeting offered a snapshot of the questions and directions shaping contemporary attention research.

While not a comprehensive overview of the entire field of visual attention research, here we synthesize several of the emerging themes from this meeting in hopes of offering a useful tool for contemporary researchers to understand some of the topics currently driving attention research, and why these questions warrant continued interest.

Contributors: Brandi Lee Drisdelle, Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld, Clayton Hickey, Dirk Kerzel, Heinrich Liesefeld, Juan Lupianez, George R. Mangun, Matt Oxner, Heleen Slagter, Dirk van Moorselaar, Alon Zivony The seminal work of Steven Hillyard and colleagues in the 1970s and 80s identified prototypical changes to evoked electrical responses measured on the scalp of participants when performing visual attention tasks, laying the foundations for a fiftyplus-year research program investigating how ERPs track visual attentional deployment (Van Voorhis & Hillyard, 1977).

Mangun, Matt Oxner, Heleen Slagter, Dirk van Moorselaar, Alon Zivony</ref> The seminal work of Steven Hillyard and colleagues in the 1970s and 80s identified prototypical changes to evoked electrical responses measured on the scalp of participants when performing visual attention tasks, laying the foundations for a fiftyplus-year research program investigating how ERPs track visual attentional deployment <ref type="bibr" target="#b270">(Van Voorhis & Hillyard, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The striking persistence of ERP-based research can largely be attributed to the temporal precision of these signals, which can track attentional processes that unravel rapidly in time, thus making them a natural complement to behavioral chronometric methods (Posner, 1978) and visual search paradigms (Treisman & Gelade, 1980) common to cognitive psychology.
text.formatted: The striking persistence of ERP-based research can largely be attributed to the temporal precision of these signals, which can track attentional processes that unravel rapidly in time, thus making them a natural complement to behavioral chronometric methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b215">(Posner, 1978)</ref> and visual search paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b256">(Treisman & Gelade, 1980)</ref> common to cognitive psychology.

text.text: Early work on cued (G. Mangun et al., 1987; G. R. Mangun & Hillyard, 1991) and reflexive attention (Hopfinger & Mangun, 1998) laid the foundation for ERP research on attentional processing.
text.formatted: Early work on cued (G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">Mangun et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">G. R. Mangun & Hillyard, 1991)</ref> and reflexive attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Hopfinger & Mangun, 1998)</ref> laid the foundation for ERP research on attentional processing.

text.text: This soon gave way to the use of more complex bilateral stimulus arrays, introduced to investigate attention mechanisms during visual search (Heinze et al., 1990; Luck & Hillyard, 1990).
text.formatted: This soon gave way to the use of more complex bilateral stimulus arrays, introduced to investigate attention mechanisms during visual search <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(Heinze et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Luck & Hillyard, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: By leveraging the spatial organization of the visual system (where stimuli presented in the left and right visual hemifields are initially processed in contralateral, or opposite, cerebral hemispheres) Hillyard and colleagues were able to isolate the electrical correlates of neural processing of items in attended and unattended hemifields; thereby allowing the study of stimulus configurations that more closely approximated natural scenes.

This lateralized approach gave rise to the discovery of two electroencephalographic components in particular that are now considered paradigmatic in the study of visual attention -the target-related N2pc and distractor-evoked P D.

First came the N2pc, a lateralized component calculated by subtracting electrical activity in ipsilateral from contralateral electrodes (usually PO7/8) relative to the location of an attended item (Luck & Hillyard, 1994a , 1994b).
text.formatted: First came the N2pc, a lateralized component calculated by subtracting electrical activity in ipsilateral from contralateral electrodes (usually PO7/8) relative to the location of an attended item <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">(Luck & Hillyard, 1994a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">, 1994b)</ref>.

text.text: This negative component reliably appeared when targets were presented among non-targets, but also sometimes in response to distractors, and has since shaped numerous research programs utilizing EEG in the study of attention.

This ERP component was complemented in 2009 by the discovery of the P D -a distractor-related ERP component occurring when distractors were presented lateralized and targets were presented on the vertical midline (where their electrical activity was equally present in both hemifields; Hickey et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This ERP component was complemented in 2009 by the discovery of the P D -a distractor-related ERP component occurring when distractors were presented lateralized and targets were presented on the vertical midline (where their electrical activity was equally present in both hemifields; <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Hickey et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Using the same electrodes as were implicated in N2pc analyses, Hickey and colleagues showed that an electroencephalographic signature of distractor suppression presented as a positivity over the contralateral hemisphere.

With the growth of research on distractor processing in recent years, the P D has come to mirror the popularity of the N2pc as a central component of many ongoing research programs (Gaspelin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: With the growth of research on distractor processing in recent years, the P D has come to mirror the popularity of the N2pc as a central component of many ongoing research programs <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Gaspelin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Today, the study of lateralized ERPs that result from attentional processingspecifically the target and distractor N2pc and the distractor P D -remains a cornerstone of EEG attention research.

These simple-to-register encephalographic components have been extensively utilized to study topics as far reaching as the divergent neural markers of schizophrenia or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children (Sawaki et al., 2017; E. Wang et al., 2016) to studies of trait anxiety or trust in AI (Gaspar & McDonald, 2018; Wiese & Feldmann-Wüstefeld, 2026).
text.formatted: These simple-to-register encephalographic components have been extensively utilized to study topics as far reaching as the divergent neural markers of schizophrenia or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b229">(Sawaki et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b277">E. Wang et al., 2016)</ref> to studies of trait anxiety or trust in AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Gaspar & McDonald, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b281">Wiese & Feldmann-Wüstefeld, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the paragraphs below, we highlight some of the newest advances in ERP methodology, as well as the open theoretical questions driving research using the N2pc and P D today.

In the original work by Luck and colleagues identifying the N2pc, the authors proposed that this negative component was the result of spatial filtering, and was thus largely reflecting a distractor-related neural process rather than pure target processing (Luck et al., 1997).
text.formatted: In the original work by Luck and colleagues identifying the N2pc, the authors proposed that this negative component was the result of spatial filtering, and was thus largely reflecting a distractor-related neural process rather than pure target processing <ref type="bibr">(Luck et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Luck and colleagues reached this conclusion based on the observation that no reliable N2pc was observed when the displays consisted solely of targets, suggesting that the component depends on some degree of spatial competition between perceptual representations (Luck & Hillyard, 1994b).
text.formatted: Luck and colleagues reached this conclusion based on the observation that no reliable N2pc was observed when the displays consisted solely of targets, suggesting that the component depends on some degree of spatial competition between perceptual representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">(Luck & Hillyard, 1994b)</ref>.

text.text: This conclusion was later challenged by Eimer (1996), who demonstrated that the N2pc was measurable when targets were presented alone in a hemifield, with a distractor presented in the opposite hemifield.
text.formatted: This conclusion was later challenged by <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Eimer (1996)</ref>, who demonstrated that the N2pc was measurable when targets were presented alone in a hemifield, with a distractor presented in the opposite hemifield.

text.text: Since this demonstration, the N2pc has been widely used as a paradigmatic index related to attentional selection, showing notable modulations in latency and amplitude based on the ease of target detection (Töllner et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Since this demonstration, the N2pc has been widely used as a paradigmatic index related to attentional selection, showing notable modulations in latency and amplitude based on the ease of target detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b255">(Töllner et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this, there remains some uncertainty about the interpretation of modulations in the N2pc, and how these are linked to attentional activity in the attended hemifield.
For the N2pc, much like many other ERPs, it is common that a specified time window is selected and lateralized activity averaged in this window with its amplitude then compared between conditions.
Typically this is the window between 200 and 300 ms post display onset, but bespoke windows are common in the literature.

However, using preset windows presumes knowledge about the size and timing of the to-bemeasured component which is justified when replicating existing work or using a paradigm with well-established ERP timing, but risks missing the ERP altogether when a novel manipulation is tested.

In a recent example of the well-known danger of predetermined window-based analyses, Constant et al. (2025) in a pre-registered ManyLabs replication of Eimer (1996) found that shape targets elicited a late N2pc almost completely out of their expected window across most datasets.
text.formatted: In a recent example of the well-known danger of predetermined window-based analyses, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Constant et al. (2025)</ref> in a pre-registered ManyLabs replication of <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Eimer (1996)</ref> found that shape targets elicited a late N2pc almost completely out of their expected window across most datasets.

text.text: The timing of the N2pc is further known to vary in line with response times in tasks where the time needed for target detection is variable trial-to-trial.

Numerous studies have compared the N2pc in efficient, parallel search tasks to inefficient, serial search tasks and noted significant differences in its shape and temporal profile (Drisdelle & Jolicoeur, 2020; Kandemir et al., 2026; Oxner, Mazza, et al., 2024) with some only registering an N2pc in inefficient search when trials were separated between fast and slow responses (Dowdall et al., 2012). Liesefeld et al. (2017) similarly found that the N2pc can be significantly delayed on trials in which a competing distractor is on the screen, observing a distractor-evoked N2pc earlier in time that then needed to be resolved before a delayed, second N2pc could be measured towards a competing target.
text.formatted: Numerous studies have compared the N2pc in efficient, parallel search tasks to inefficient, serial search tasks and noted significant differences in its shape and temporal profile <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Drisdelle & Jolicoeur, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Kandemir et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b210">Oxner, Mazza, et al., 2024)</ref> with some only registering an N2pc in inefficient search when trials were separated between fast and slow responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Dowdall et al., 2012)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Liesefeld et al. (2017)</ref> similarly found that the N2pc can be significantly delayed on trials in which a competing distractor is on the screen, observing a distractor-evoked N2pc earlier in time that then needed to be resolved before a delayed, second N2pc could be measured towards a competing target.

text.text: In these examples, the use of a set N2pc window will fail to register temporal variability between conditions, and simply register an attenuated N2pc in certain conditions.

However, the alternative approach of simply selecting a window based on visual inspection following data collection faces issues of post-hoc data sorting (i.e. the risk of manufacturing effects from inherently noisy data; Luck & Gaspelin, 2017).
text.formatted: However, the alternative approach of simply selecting a window based on visual inspection following data collection faces issues of post-hoc data sorting (i.e. the risk of manufacturing effects from inherently noisy data; <ref type="bibr" target="#b168">Luck & Gaspelin, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, datadriven alternatives to the predetermined window approach such as the latency estimate technique (Liesefeld, 2018) or residue iteration decomposition (RIDE; Ouyang et al., 2011), offer compelling alternatives to this approach which may better capture a temporally variable N2pc while remaining methodologically sound.
text.formatted: Rather, datadriven alternatives to the predetermined window approach such as the latency estimate technique <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">(Liesefeld, 2018)</ref> or residue iteration decomposition (RIDE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b207">Ouyang et al., 2011)</ref>, offer compelling alternatives to this approach which may better capture a temporally variable N2pc while remaining methodologically sound.

text.text: Overall, these new data-driven approaches present an improvement over traditional predetermined windows with little-to-no drawbacks and thus the project to standardize these techniques remains timely.
It additionally remains a clear and worthwhile topic to explore what precise cognitive process the N2pc actually indexes, and what this says about the putative mechanism of attention itself.

Notwithstanding debates about the meaning of "attention" (Hommel et al., 2019; W. Wu, 2024; Zivony & Eimer, 2022; Woodman, 2026), it is clear that the N2pc indexes a cognitive process closely related to the allocation of attention in space.
text.formatted: Notwithstanding debates about the meaning of "attention" <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">(Hommel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b288">W. Wu, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b299">Zivony & Eimer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b286">Woodman, 2026)</ref>, it is clear that the N2pc indexes a cognitive process closely related to the allocation of attention in space.

text.text: However, a growing consensus emerged that the N2pc reflects a process that occurs further downstream, and may not even emerge under conditions where attentional shifting is observed (Woodman et al., 2009; Giattino et al., 2018; Rashal et al., 2022; Talcott et al., 2025; Zivony et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, a growing consensus emerged that the N2pc reflects a process that occurs further downstream, and may not even emerge under conditions where attentional shifting is observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b287">(Woodman et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Giattino et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Rashal et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b246">Talcott et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b298">Zivony et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This begs the question: what precise cognitive process does the N2pc follow from?
It is uncontroversial to point out that the N2pc does not reflect salience processing per se, as evident by its relatively late occurrence (arising usually 200-300 ms following stimulus onset).

Instead, a body of work has now implicated this component as relating to object individuation, perhaps representing a stage of attentional processing where objects are separated from their backgrounds (D. E. Anderson et al., 2013; Foster et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Instead, a body of work has now implicated this component as relating to object individuation, perhaps representing a stage of attentional processing where objects are separated from their backgrounds (D. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Anderson et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Foster et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for this comes from observations that the N2pc is reliably modulated by the number of salient targets in a hemifield, revealing a role for object individuation and subitizing for the N2pc (Mazza, 2017; Mazza et al., 2013; Mazza & Caramazza, 2015).
text.formatted: Evidence for this comes from observations that the N2pc is reliably modulated by the number of salient targets in a hemifield, revealing a role for object individuation and subitizing for the N2pc <ref type="bibr" target="#b186">(Mazza, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b188">Mazza et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b187">Mazza & Caramazza, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this, recent work using concurrently recorded EEG and fMRI noted that N2pc modulations robustly predicted the emergence of object category information in the fMRI signal, indicating that the N2pc marked some passage of object-related information from the early visual system to higher object processing areas (Acunzo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Building on this, recent work using concurrently recorded EEG and fMRI noted that N2pc modulations robustly predicted the emergence of object category information in the fMRI signal, indicating that the N2pc marked some passage of object-related information from the early visual system to higher object processing areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Acunzo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore the observation that a distractor-driven N2pc reliably occurs when distractors share potential target features (Luck & Hillyard, 1994a , 1994b) suggests that the N2pc is driven in part by target-template matching and indicates that it may be useful in elucidating the flexibility of attentional templates based on current task demands (i.e. Yu et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Furthermore the observation that a distractor-driven N2pc reliably occurs when distractors share potential target features <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">(Luck & Hillyard, 1994a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">, 1994b)</ref> suggests that the N2pc is driven in part by target-template matching and indicates that it may be useful in elucidating the flexibility of attentional templates based on current task demands (i.e. <ref type="bibr" target="#b292">Yu et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The discourse on what component of attentional processing the N2pc precisely indexes highlights that visual attention consists of multiple stages, and that these stages remain poorly characterized.

Already existing work has shown that the N2pc is influenced differentially by early (distractor salience) and late (distractor-target similarity) processing demands of a task (Aubin & Jolicoeur, 2016; Drisdelle & Jolicoeur, 2018).
text.formatted: Already existing work has shown that the N2pc is influenced differentially by early (distractor salience) and late (distractor-target similarity) processing demands of a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Aubin & Jolicoeur, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Drisdelle & Jolicoeur, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Pinning down precisely what attentional process the N2pc indexes may thus make it an essential tool in future research at characterizing the processing steps that make up visual attention, and thereby may aid in the larger challenge of arriving at a precise definition of attention itself.
Several decades of N2pc focused research has clearly demonstrated the utility of this easily detected lateralized component for measuring attentional processing in space.
Both methodological improvements in the measure of the N2pc, as well as further work testing the boundary conditions in which an N2pc is measurable are worthwhile research endeavors.

Additionally, the combination of the N2pc with other EEG measures (e.g. multivariate spatial or feature decoding) can offer even greater insights into the cognitive processes that drive this paradigmatic index of attentional processing.
Similar debate surrounds the interpretation of positive polarity components that often precede, follow, or replace a distractor-driven N2pc.

Modulations of the P D seem clearly related to distractor handling, as a reduced P D has reliably been associated with better suppression due to spatial cueing (van Zoest et al., 2021), learning (Hanne et al., 2025; van Moorselaar et al., 2020), target-distractor distance (Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2021; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2022) or simply due to less distracting distractors (Chen et al., 2023; Feldmann-Wüstefeld & Vogel, 2019; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2019).

text.text: Furthermore, combining ERP approaches with inverted encoding models reveals the P D coincides with below-baseline processing spatially localized at the distractor location, directly linking the component to spatial suppression (Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Furthermore, combining ERP approaches with inverted encoding models reveals the P D coincides with below-baseline processing spatially localized at the distractor location, directly linking the component to spatial suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, concerns that the P D merely indexes an N2pc to the opposite hemifield are partially assuaged by studies finding a P D in conditions where no nontarget appears contralateral to the distractor (e.g. Drisdelle & Eimer, 2021; Hickey et al., 2009; van Zoest et al., 2021; Weaver et al., 2017; Wu & Fu, 2017;  but this doesn't mean that the P D is never an N2pc to contralateral nontargets, i.e. Kerzel & Burra, 2020; Kerzel & Huynh Cong, 2023; Tam et al., 2022) However, interpretations of the P D are complicated by the possibility of a cooccurring distractor-N2pc which overlaps roughly in time with the P D in many experimental paradigms and presents in an opposite polarity (see Gaspelin et al., 2023 for a review).

text.text: As such, modulations in the P D amplitude could well be the result of an overlapping negative-polarity N2pc component present at the same time and electrodes, causing destructive averaging of both signals (Forschack et al., 2022a; Oxner et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As such, modulations in the P D amplitude could well be the result of an overlapping negative-polarity N2pc component present at the same time and electrodes, causing destructive averaging of both signals <ref type="bibr">(Forschack et al., 2022a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b211">Oxner et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Often, the amplitude of the P D and distractor-evoked N2pc covary, with a distractor-evoked N2pc preceding and delaying the P D (Feldmann-Wüstefeld, 2021; Feldmann-Wüstefeld & Schubö, 2013).

text.text: This suggests that greater attentional capture elicits correspondingly greater reactive suppression and supports a serial processing characterization of the visual system (Liesefeld et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This suggests that greater attentional capture elicits correspondingly greater reactive suppression and supports a serial processing characterization of the visual system <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">(Liesefeld et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, if capture by a salient distractor only occurs on half of all trials, this may produce an overlapping distractor-N2pc with the P D in the trial aggregate, presenting a risk of destructive averaging.

One potentially useful method for tying ERP modulations to behavior is linear mixed-effects models, which provide single trial outputs that do not require averaging across the dataset, and so can potentially remedy issues related to trial averaging (Henare et al., 2024; Hickey et al., 2025; Oxner, Mazza, et al., 2024).

text.text: Furthermore, recent research has proposed that multivariate approaches can be used to effectively isolate univariate neural signals in noisy data, allowing researchers to disentangle and isolate canonical ERPs from overlapping neural signals (Weindel et al., 2024).

text.text: Cross decoding using multivariate decoders trained on one trial type and tested on another further offers another compelling method of detecting cognitive processes otherwise obscured by noisy data (Kandemir et al., 2026; Z. Zhang & Lewis-Peacock, 2024).

Zhang & Lewis-Peacock, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It remains to be seen what new novel insights related to the distractor suppression and the P D will arise in the coming years by leveraging these new analysis approaches to unveil previously undetectable cognitive phenomena.

While the P D is widely viewed as a marker of suppression, some studies observe a much earlier distractor-driven positivity, which some research groups refer to as the early-P D and interpret as a marker of proactive suppression (Sawaki & Luck, 2010; Drisdelle & Eimer, 2021 , 2023; Gaspelin & Luck, 2018a; Redding & Fiebelkorn, 2024; Stilwell et al., 2022; B. Wang et al., 2019; Weaver et al., 2017).

Wang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b279">Weaver et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, a number of research groups have pointed out that this early positivity exactly overlaps with the Posterior Positivity Contralateral component (Ppc) which has traditionally been thought to index raw salience processing (Burra & Kerzel, 2014; Corriveau et al., 2012).
text.formatted: However, a number of research groups have pointed out that this early positivity exactly overlaps with the Posterior Positivity Contralateral component (Ppc) which has traditionally been thought to index raw salience processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Burra & Kerzel, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Corriveau et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: As such, it is an open question whether the early-P D truly represents a unique neural process to the Ppc, with unique neural populations and functions roughly overlapping in space and timing, or whether this early positivity is simply a well-known salience signal that also often appears with a salient distractor (Sawaki & Luck, 2010).
text.formatted: As such, it is an open question whether the early-P D truly represents a unique neural process to the Ppc, with unique neural populations and functions roughly overlapping in space and timing, or whether this early positivity is simply a well-known salience signal that also often appears with a salient distractor <ref type="bibr" target="#b230">(Sawaki & Luck, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work has supported the latter assertion: showing that the early distractor positivity is present in cases where suppression is absent and therefore evoked by salient targets (McDonald et al., 2026; Oxner, Mazza, et al., 2024; Oxner et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work has supported the latter assertion: showing that the early distractor positivity is present in cases where suppression is absent and therefore evoked by salient targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">(McDonald et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b210">Oxner, Mazza, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b211">Oxner et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, this early component has been found to be sensitive to target regularities (van Moorselaar et al., 2023) and research using learned suppression paradigms have failed to find modulations in this early component to match that which has reliably been found in its late-occurring counterpart (Hanne et al., 2025; van Moorselaar et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Furthermore, this early component has been found to be sensitive to target regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b265">(van Moorselaar et al., 2023)</ref> and research using learned suppression paradigms have failed to find modulations in this early component to match that which has reliably been found in its late-occurring counterpart <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Hanne et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Moorselaar et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, concerns about an overlapping N2pc nearby in timing are even larger for the early positivity which is reliably lower in amplitude than the later P D -meaning even an infrequent adjacent N2pc may be sufficient to obliterate this positivity from the signal after trial averaging.
What is clear is that much remains to be learned about the lateralized positivity that often follows the presentation of a salient distractor over the contralateral hemisphere.
It remains to be seen how clever experimentation combined with methodological advances will allow researchers to better disentangle the underlying cognitive operations driving the P D .

Clearly this is just the beginning of this research program and work in the coming years will allow us to better understand how a positive deflection following the presentation of a lateral distractor indexes the cognitive mechanisms of distractor handling.
The already-long history of ERP research on visual attention attests to the technique's durable appeal.

The relatively low barrier to entry for ERP research, which requires only minimal experimental setups and is therefore feasible even for labs with limited resources, together with its ability to reveal patterns of cognitive processing that are not evident in overt behavior, makes it an especially appealing tool in the attention researcher's arsenal.

Building on over three decades of work, ERP research is at an exciting and optimistic place, as new methodological advances allow researchers to ask ever more probing questions in the pursuit of a better understanding of human visual attention.
Open questions about the precise cognitive mechanisms indexed by these ERPs further represent compelling topics of interest that will continue to drive research programs in the years to come.foot_0

text.text: Contributors: Kabir Arora, Samson Chota, Oscar Ferrante, Surya Gayet, Eelke Spaak, Stefan Van der Stigchel For many decades, frequency tagging has offered a powerful method of tracking attentional allocation with unambiguous origins relative to the measurement of endogenous oscillations in the brain (for debates on the latter, see : Antonov et al., 2020; Bonnefond & Jensen, 2024; Jensen & Bonnefond, 2026; Schneider et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Contributors: <ref type="bibr">Kabir Arora, Samson Chota, Oscar Ferrante, Surya Gayet, Eelke Spaak, Stefan Van der Stigchel</ref> For many decades, frequency tagging has offered a powerful method of tracking attentional allocation with unambiguous origins relative to the measurement of endogenous oscillations in the brain (for debates on the latter, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">: Antonov et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Bonnefond & Jensen, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Jensen & Bonnefond, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b234">Schneider et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: By flickering stimuli at set frequencies, neural responses as recorded in M/EEG will show distinct peaks in the power spectrum at these stimulated frequencies.

These steady state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) are further known to be modulated by attention such that if attention is directed to an item 'tagged' at a certain frequency, then the spectral peak will be enhanced at this frequency (M. M. Müller, Picton, et al., 1998; M. M. Müller, Teder-Sälejärvi, et al., 1998; M. M. Müller et al., 2003).
text.formatted: These steady state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) are further known to be modulated by attention such that if attention is directed to an item 'tagged' at a certain frequency, then the spectral peak will be enhanced at this frequency (M. M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">Müller, Picton, et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr">M. M. Müller, Teder-Sälejärvi, et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b197">M. M. Müller et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Frequency tagging has thus proven to be a useful tool for measuring visual attention.
However, the use of slow, overt SSVEPs creates significant visual disturbances on the stimulus screen.

This is often undesirable as it can disrupt or significantly influence ongoing cognitive activity (Alais et al., 2016; Cass et al., 2011), fundamentally altering the bottom-up characteristics of a display with opaque consequences.
text.formatted: This is often undesirable as it can disrupt or significantly influence ongoing cognitive activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Alais et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Cass et al., 2011)</ref>, fundamentally altering the bottom-up characteristics of a display with opaque consequences.

text.text: The inherent visibility of traditional, slow SSVEPs has precluded its use in more naturalistic stimuli, or in studies seeking to measure the role of attention in multisensory environments (where significant visual disturbances may unnaturally bias attention towards visual modalities).
Furthermore, this inherent visibility has precluded the use of slow SSVEPs in the study of 'object-free' spatial attention.

Recent advances in display technology and improved M/EEG signal clarity have led to the development of Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT; Drijvers et al., 2021; Seijdel et al., 2023; Zhigalov et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Recent advances in display technology and improved M/EEG signal clarity have led to the development of Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Drijvers et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">Seijdel et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b296">Zhigalov et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: By pushing frequency tagging into the highfrequency range (typically between 55 and 75 Hz), stimuli flicker so fast that the tag becomes imperceptible yet still evokes a measurable oscillatory response in the early visual cortex (Spaak et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By pushing frequency tagging into the highfrequency range (typically between 55 and 75 Hz), stimuli flicker so fast that the tag becomes imperceptible yet still evokes a measurable oscillatory response in the early visual cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b239">(Spaak et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, the resulting oscillatory neural signals have been shown to reliably modulate with attention such that attended items display higher power/coherence values than unattended items (Arora et al., 2025; Zhigalov et al., 2019; Zhigalov & Jensen, 2020), thereby opening the door for RIFT as a subtle method of detecting neural modulations as a result of covert attention.
text.formatted: Crucially, the resulting oscillatory neural signals have been shown to reliably modulate with attention such that attended items display higher power/coherence values than unattended items <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Arora et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b296">Zhigalov et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b297">Zhigalov & Jensen, 2020)</ref>, thereby opening the door for RIFT as a subtle method of detecting neural modulations as a result of covert attention.

text.text: A fundamental, longstanding question in attention research is: when does spatial attention proactively boost early visual processing at the attended location (i.e., enhance cortical excitability in early visual cortex), and when does it instead only reactively enhance the response to a stimulus once it appears at the attended location (i.e., upon evoking an object representation, and likely further down the processing pathway)?

Distinguishing between proactive spatial (object-free) and reactive stimulus driven (object-based) attention requires probing of attentional enhancement at specific locations invisibly, in the absence of any discernable object at those locations. Arora et al. (2025) successfully dissociated these two types of attentional processing by utilizing RIFT to probe spatial excitability invisibly, demonstrating a new way to probe cortical excitability without any object presentation at all. Arora et al. (2025) found that cuing a region in space (where a memory target would soon be presented) resulted in elevated RIFT signal at the cued location, indexing enhanced attentional processing.
text.formatted: Distinguishing between proactive spatial (object-free) and reactive stimulus driven (object-based) attention requires probing of attentional enhancement at specific locations invisibly, in the absence of any discernable object at those locations. <ref type="bibr">Arora et al. (2025)</ref> successfully dissociated these two types of attentional processing by utilizing RIFT to probe spatial excitability invisibly, demonstrating a new way to probe cortical excitability without any object presentation at all. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Arora et al. (2025)</ref> found that cuing a region in space (where a memory target would soon be presented) resulted in elevated RIFT signal at the cued location, indexing enhanced attentional processing.

text.text: Notably, this enhanced RIFT response was not observed in a slightly different design where the spatial cue indicated which of two previously presented memory targets is relevant for subsequent recall.

This finding showcases a sharp divergence with alpha responses -a classical, endogenous oscillatory marker of attention -which showed an enhanced lateralized response following the spatial cue in both situations. Arora et al. (2025) is one example of a key feature of RIFT that opens new lines of inquiry that were previously closed: by allowing researchers to invisibly probe the visual system, the neural consequences of (covert) spatial attention can now be probed separately from higher order processing.
text.formatted: This finding showcases a sharp divergence with alpha responses -a classical, endogenous oscillatory marker of attention -which showed an enhanced lateralized response following the spatial cue in both situations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Arora et al. (2025)</ref> is one example of a key feature of RIFT that opens new lines of inquiry that were previously closed: by allowing researchers to invisibly probe the visual system, the neural consequences of (covert) spatial attention can now be probed separately from higher order processing.

text.text: Moreover, RIFT is easily split into multiple tagging signals, allowing researchers to tile the visual field with dissociable RIFT probes to measure how attentional enhancement waxes, wanes and shifts across the visual field in time.

For instance, Wang et al. (2026) used RIFT across multiple locations to probe how top-down and bottom-up attention dynamically compete in an experiment using the additional singleton task (Theeuwes, 1992).
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b276">Wang et al. (2026)</ref> used RIFT across multiple locations to probe how top-down and bottom-up attention dynamically compete in an experiment using the additional singleton task <ref type="bibr" target="#b249">(Theeuwes, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: They observed higher RIFT evoked signals for both targets and distractors relative to neutral nontargets, reflecting the influence of top-down goals and bottom-up salience on early visual processing.
Importantly, the presence of a distractor attenuated the initial RIFT response to the target, indicating competition during the earliest stages of visual processing.
Over time, however, RIFT responses to the distractor decreased below responses to both targets and nontargets, consistent with reactive suppression of task-irrelevant stimuli.

RIFT can be an important technique for answering a central question in the study of selection history: whether learned suppression is proactive or reactive in nature (for a more in depth discussion on this topic, see the below section on the role of learning in shaping attentional deployment).

Because RIFT can track placeholder locations without altering their salience, it provides an ideal tool to probe preparatory neural responses before the onset of the search display. Ferrante et al. (2023) tested the hypothesis that statistical learning of distractor locations relies on proactive spatial suppression.
text.formatted: Because RIFT can track placeholder locations without altering their salience, it provides an ideal tool to probe preparatory neural responses before the onset of the search display. <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Ferrante et al. (2023)</ref> tested the hypothesis that statistical learning of distractor locations relies on proactive spatial suppression.

text.text: By tagging placeholder stimuli before a search array appeared, they observed weaker RIFT responses in the pre-stimulus window for locations with a high probability of containing a distractor.
These insights provide some of the first direct neural evidence that suppression can indeed operate proactively.

RIFT's ability to invisibly map shifts in cortical sensitivity across the visual field further allows for measuring other features of attentional processing -such as observing how attention moves through space, and whether it expands or contracts given current task demands.
Furthermore, continuing advances in presentation and analysis techniques allow to simultaneously tag an increasing number of spatial locations or (static and even moving) stimuli.

The option to measure RIFT responses within visible placeholders versus on a uniform background additionally offers researchers the unique opportunity to observe the role of objects in attention measurement, capitalizing on the visual system's inherent design to aid in object processing.

Perhaps the greatest untapped application of RIFT is in naturalistic stimuli, where spatially specific attentional measurements are now possible without disturbing the visual scene itself, allowing for the neural tracking of attention in natural environments in a neutral manner with a level of flexibility which was previously impossible.
Given it remains a relatively new technique, caution remains called for when interpreting modulations in RIFT signals given how much remains unknown about its precise cortical origins.

Work using MEG has localized the RIFT response to the early visual system (Ferrante et al., 2023; Zhigalov et al., 2019; Zhigalov & Jensen, 2020), suggesting it is a tool for measuring early cortical processing shifts as a function of spatial attention.
text.formatted: Work using MEG has localized the RIFT response to the early visual system <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Ferrante et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b296">Zhigalov et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b297">Zhigalov & Jensen, 2020)</ref>, suggesting it is a tool for measuring early cortical processing shifts as a function of spatial attention.

text.text: Concurrent EEG/fMRI studies have similarly localized slower SSVEPs in V1, but also notably find origins from later processing areas such as V2/3 (Di Russo et al., 2007; Mohr et al., 2024) and hMT (Boylan et al., 2023), suggesting modulations in lower frequency flicker may capture distinct cognitive processes from its high frequency counterpart.
text.formatted: Concurrent EEG/fMRI studies have similarly localized slower SSVEPs in V1, but also notably find origins from later processing areas such as V2/3 (Di <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Russo et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b192">Mohr et al., 2024)</ref> and hMT <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Boylan et al., 2023)</ref>, suggesting modulations in lower frequency flicker may capture distinct cognitive processes from its high frequency counterpart.

text.text: It remains further unclear how/whether the RIFT signal captures different cognitive processes than traditional, slower SSVEPs.
While the spatial sensitivity of RIFT is well established, it remains unclear whether RIFT tracks feature based attention similar to slow SSVEPs.

It was recently demonstrated that RIFT can indeed capture feature-based attention in a guided visual search task, thereby demonstrating its utility in top-down search (Bouwkamp et al., 2024; Duecker et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It was recently demonstrated that RIFT can indeed capture feature-based attention in a guided visual search task, thereby demonstrating its utility in top-down search <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Bouwkamp et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Duecker et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, both these studies used a T among L's task, in which attention was directed at discrete items at specific locations in space.
This differs from the more distributed attention typically measured in feature-based attention tasks such as random dot kinematograms (S. Andersen & Müller, 2010; M. Müller et al., 2006).
text.formatted: This differs from the more distributed attention typically measured in feature-based attention tasks such as random dot kinematograms (S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Andersen & Müller, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b195">M. Müller et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: It therefore remains unclear whether RIFT signals produce comparable results to those often observed in traditional random dot kinematogram studies.

Furthermore, while some effects observed using slow SSVEPs have been replicated using RIFT (e.g.: Forschack et al., 2022; D. Wang et al., 2026), other effects have not (e.g.: Duncan et al., 2025; Ferrante et al., 2023), suggesting that the neural processes indexed by RIFT and traditional, slower SSVEPs may originate from different neuronal populations; highlighting the importance of understanding this divergence as RIFT gains popularity.
text.formatted: Furthermore, while some effects observed using slow SSVEPs have been replicated using RIFT (e.g.: <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Forschack et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b276">D. Wang et al., 2026)</ref>, other effects have not (e.g.: <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Duncan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Ferrante et al., 2023)</ref>, suggesting that the neural processes indexed by RIFT and traditional, slower SSVEPs may originate from different neuronal populations; highlighting the importance of understanding this divergence as RIFT gains popularity.

text.text: For these reasons, more work is clearly needed to better understand the locus of RIFT modulations, as well as what precise cognitive mechanisms it responds to.

Source localization using MEG is a known and powerful tool for isolating cortical loci, and recent advances in optically pumped magnetometers (OPM) have the potential for improved source localization over traditional cryogenic MEG (Boto et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2025; Nugent et al., 2022), perhaps offering a better method of tracking the locus of the RIFT signal.
text.formatted: Source localization using MEG is a known and powerful tool for isolating cortical loci, and recent advances in optically pumped magnetometers (OPM) have the potential for improved source localization over traditional cryogenic MEG <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Boto et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b158">Liang et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b201">Nugent et al., 2022)</ref>, perhaps offering a better method of tracking the locus of the RIFT signal.

text.text: Additionally, comparing fMRI modulations and M/EEG RIFT coherence could unlock further insights into the spatial origins of RIFT signals recorded in M/EEG, thereby improving our interpretation of RIFT modulations and their functional significance.
The possibility of deploying both slow SSVEPs and RIFT at the same time within an experiment trial further may offer crucial insights into how these signals diverge in their sensitivities.
RIFT offers the chance to answer compelling questions about the human attention system that have previously been impossible or convoluted to probe.

Most critically, the externally evoked nature of the RIFT signal (originating on an external computer screen rather than an opaque neural process) gives a straightforward and elegant measure of attentional processing which previously demanded the accompanying visual disturbances of SSVEP techniques.

While still a young technique, RIFT has already revolutionized the study of attention in reading, where its invisible measurement allows researchers to capture the movement of attention undisturbed while participants parse complex symbols (Pan et al., 2021 (Pan et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: While still a young technique, RIFT has already revolutionized the study of attention in reading, where its invisible measurement allows researchers to capture the movement of attention undisturbed while participants parse complex symbols <ref type="bibr" target="#b213">(Pan et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b212">(Pan et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: Future research avenues include the application of RIFT to studies with natural or dynamic scene stimuli, where locations or objects can be invisibly tagged and attention tracked unobtrusively.

RIFT additionally has clear applicability in brain computer interfaces, where the ability to track attentional deployment without disturbing the visual experience may offer an ideal method of hands-free control (Brickwedde et al., 2022).
text.formatted: RIFT additionally has clear applicability in brain computer interfaces, where the ability to track attentional deployment without disturbing the visual experience may offer an ideal method of hands-free control <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Brickwedde et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While the early work on RIFT used MEG and presented stimuli on high precision projectors at high refresh rates (1440 Hz), recent work has shown that RIFT is also measurable using EEG (Arora et al., 2024 (Arora et al., , 2025) ) and can be entrained even using commercially available high-performance gaming monitors with lower refresh rates than a Propixx (Çelik et al., 2025; Dimigen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: While the early work on RIFT used MEG and presented stimuli on high precision projectors at high refresh rates (1440 Hz), recent work has shown that RIFT is also measurable using EEG <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Arora et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Arora et al., , 2025) )</ref> and can be entrained even using commercially available high-performance gaming monitors with lower refresh rates than a Propixx <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Çelik et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Dimigen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A recently published comprehensive "How to RIFT" manual paper (Arora et al., 2026) further increases accessibility of RIFT to a broad range of researchers.
text.formatted: A recently published comprehensive "How to RIFT" manual paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Arora et al., 2026)</ref> further increases accessibility of RIFT to a broad range of researchers.

text.text: Beyond researchers interested in studying attention per se, any group with a functioning M/EEG lab can now implement RIFT in their existing computer-based task, allowing to track (and control) for differences in attention over space/stimuli and time.

These advances have demonstrated that RIFT is a technique with a significantly lower bar of entry than was initially assumed and thus may soon come to be a major mode of attentional measurement used in encephalography in labs across the world.
For decades, ocular behavior has been treated primarily as a nuisance in encephalographic studies of the brain.

Because participants naturally tend to move their eyes toward the object of current attention, eye movements present a major confound when recording brain activity: any evoked response might simply reflect the muscular activity necessary to perform a saccade or the retinal displacement of an image following one.

Consequently, removing eye artifacts has been an important step in data collection and preprocessing, involving stringent participant instruction to maintain fixation, careful trimming of eye-tracking data around saccades, or regressing out ocular signals via independent component analyses.
However, a major current topic driving modern encephalographic research is the dramatic reversal of this trend.
Instead of eliminating ocular behavior to study 'pure' covert attention, researchers are now actively interrogating the crucial interplay between the oculomotor system and covert neural signals.

This shift is motivated by action-oriented accounts, such as the premotor theory of attention (Rizzolatti et al., 1987), which conceptualize attention not merely as a sensory filter, but as a mechanism deeply tied to covert motor planning and goal-directed action selection (Koevoet et al., 2023 (Koevoet et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: This shift is motivated by action-oriented accounts, such as the premotor theory of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b222">(Rizzolatti et al., 1987)</ref>, which conceptualize attention not merely as a sensory filter, but as a mechanism deeply tied to covert motor planning and goal-directed action selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">(Koevoet et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">(Koevoet et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: The connection between attention and planned action is a strong one, with neuroimaging work demonstrating that activation patterns within the frontoparietal network during attention tasks vary depending on the type of movement that can be prepared (e.g., saccades vs. grasping), even in the absence of overt movement or motor imagery (Craighero et al., 1999).
text.formatted: The connection between attention and planned action is a strong one, with neuroimaging work demonstrating that activation patterns within the frontoparietal network during attention tasks vary depending on the type of movement that can be prepared (e.g., saccades vs. grasping), even in the absence of overt movement or motor imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Craighero et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Within visual attention, eye movements are an essential component of the spatial attention network as often covert spatial attention precedes the movement of the eye to foveate on the current target of attention (Deubel & Schneider, 1996; Kowler et al., 1995; Rolfs & Carrasco, 2012).
text.formatted: Within visual attention, eye movements are an essential component of the spatial attention network as often covert spatial attention precedes the movement of the eye to foveate on the current target of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Deubel & Schneider, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">Kowler et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b224">Rolfs & Carrasco, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Leading some to wonder what rich attentional information can be recorded by looking at ocular behavior, and to what degree these simple measurements can complement/replace encephalographic measures.
Two measures in particular have recently gained traction as useful supplementary measures of neural activity -microsaccades and pupil size.
Both in turn face challenges as the ongoing research attempts to elucidate the degree to which these measures supplement neural activity or alternatively drive the signals picked up in neuroimaging.

Early indications show promise that these overt markers of attentional processing may not directly interfere with EEG signals, and may thus come to be a useful analogue to the effects measured from the brain.
When studying the neural basis of covert voluntary attention, a vital prerequisite is ensuring that visual stimulation-as registered by the retina-remains identical across conditions.
Yet, humans actively sample their environment.
Even during attempted fixation, humans continuously make microsaccades and experience pupil fluctuations (Martinez-Conde et al., 2004; Rolfs, 2009; Ruuskanen & Mathot, 2026).
text.formatted: Even during attempted fixation, humans continuously make microsaccades and experience pupil fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">(Martinez-Conde et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b223">Rolfs, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b226">Ruuskanen & Mathot, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because these micro-scale eye behaviors alter how visual inputs impinge on the retina, a fundamental question is currently driving the field: are classical neural markers of covert attention actually driven by 'bottom-up' sensory changes caused by these subtle eye behaviors?

For instance, voluntary shifts of spatial attention spatially bias microsaccades (Engbert & Kliegl, 2003; Hafed & Clark, 2002), even when attention is directed inward to representations held in visual working memory (Liu & van Ede, 2025; Van Ede et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For instance, voluntary shifts of spatial attention spatially bias microsaccades <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Engbert & Kliegl, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Hafed & Clark, 2002)</ref>, even when attention is directed inward to representations held in visual working memory <ref type="bibr">(Liu & van Ede, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b263">Van Ede et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Eye movements have also come under scrutiny when trying to decode the feature content of working memory from EEG signals, as studies show that features like orientation can be decoded from eye data alone (Mostert et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Eye movements have also come under scrutiny when trying to decode the feature content of working memory from EEG signals, as studies show that features like orientation can be decoded from eye data alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b194">(Mostert et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, recent work has separately shown for both the N2pc and alpha lateralization (two paradigmatic measures of covert attentional shifts) that while highly correlated to microsaccades, these well-known markers of covert attention cannot be wholly explained by these small eye movements (Liu et al., 2022 (Liu et al., , 2025;; Meyberg et al., 2017; Popov, 2026), and thus are more likely a shared downstream output resulting from shifts of attention.
text.formatted: Importantly, recent work has separately shown for both the N2pc and alpha lateralization (two paradigmatic measures of covert attentional shifts) that while highly correlated to microsaccades, these well-known markers of covert attention cannot be wholly explained by these small eye movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(Liu et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Liu et al., , 2025;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">Meyberg et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">Popov, 2026)</ref>, and thus are more likely a shared downstream output resulting from shifts of attention.

text.text: Microsaccades have further been shown to largely index shifts of attention, but fail to capture sustained attention towards a spatial location (van Harmelen & van Ede, 2025), and while attention alters the direction of microsaccades, attentional shifts do not themselves cause microsaccades (Liu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Microsaccades have further been shown to largely index shifts of attention, but fail to capture sustained attention towards a spatial location <ref type="bibr" target="#b264">(van Harmelen & van Ede, 2025)</ref>, and while attention alters the direction of microsaccades, attentional shifts do not themselves cause microsaccades <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">(Liu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, attentional shifts simply bias the direction of microsaccades that would have occurred anyway, even if a non-attentional task was performed -a pattern of results consistent with the idea that microsaccades are a downstream process sharing the same upstream origins as common EEG markers of attention.

As such, the future of microsaccadic research should treat these minute eye movements as a complementary measure to those recorded using EEG rather than solely as an alternative explanation to the patterns observed in the EEG signal (van Ede, 2026).
text.formatted: As such, the future of microsaccadic research should treat these minute eye movements as a complementary measure to those recorded using EEG rather than solely as an alternative explanation to the patterns observed in the EEG signal <ref type="bibr" target="#b262">(van Ede, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Just as microsaccades offer a window into spatial attention, pupillometry offers insights into the intensity of visual processing (Mathôt, 2018; Strauch et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Just as microsaccades offer a window into spatial attention, pupillometry offers insights into the intensity of visual processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b182">(Mathôt, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b243">Strauch et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The expansion and contraction of the pupil changes the content of visual information passing through the visual system, thus altering the eventual representation of this visual input in the brain.

It has already been noted that covert attentional demands can influence pupil dilation (Vilotijević & Mathôt, 2023), improve sensitivity in nearthreshold detection (Eberhardt et al., 2022; Mathôt & Ivanov, 2019; Ruuskanen et al., 2025) and increase SSVEP amplitudes recorded from the scalp (Suzuki et al., 2019).
text.formatted: It has already been noted that covert attentional demands can influence pupil dilation <ref type="bibr">(Vilotijević & Mathôt, 2023)</ref>, improve sensitivity in nearthreshold detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Eberhardt et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">Mathôt & Ivanov, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b225">Ruuskanen et al., 2025)</ref> and increase SSVEP amplitudes recorded from the scalp <ref type="bibr" target="#b245">(Suzuki et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It is thus essential to ascertain the degree to which changes to the pupil cause or alter brain dynamics recorded via encephalography.
In a recent study, Mathôt et al. (2023) manipulated covert visual attention and pupil size orthogonally in a single task to observe their interactions.
text.formatted: In a recent study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">Mathôt et al. (2023)</ref> manipulated covert visual attention and pupil size orthogonally in a single task to observe their interactions.

text.text: Mathôt et al. found that while attentional manipulations had clear effects on the alpha and theta frequencies, pupil size primarily modulated beta frequencies.

Furthermore, a study by Ruuskanen et al. (2025) using a visual detection task found that while pupil size reliably predicted detection performance, alpha and beta power did not, suggesting that, in this paradigm at least, the improvement in detection performance was driven by an optical effect and not the result of changes in endogenous brain states (Ruuskanen & Mathot, 2026).
text.formatted: Furthermore, a study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b225">Ruuskanen et al. (2025)</ref> using a visual detection task found that while pupil size reliably predicted detection performance, alpha and beta power did not, suggesting that, in this paradigm at least, the improvement in detection performance was driven by an optical effect and not the result of changes in endogenous brain states <ref type="bibr" target="#b226">(Ruuskanen & Mathot, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, while it is appealing to attribute improvements in performance to increased visual sensitivity derived from larger pupils, pupil size is also associated with arousal (Bradley et al., 2008; Hess & Polt, 1960; Kahneman & Beatty, 1966).
text.formatted: Importantly, while it is appealing to attribute improvements in performance to increased visual sensitivity derived from larger pupils, pupil size is also associated with arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Bradley et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Hess & Polt, 1960;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Kahneman & Beatty, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: Since arousal in turn affects performance as well as EEG markers, this is another route through which correlations between pupil size, behavior, and EEG markers may arise (reviewed in Ruuskanen & Mathôt¸ in press).
text.formatted: Since arousal in turn affects performance as well as EEG markers, this is another route through which correlations between pupil size, behavior, and EEG markers may arise (reviewed in <ref type="bibr">Ruuskanen & Mathôt¸ in press)</ref>.

text.text: Further work disentangling the relationship between pupil size, performance, and arousal thus remains needed.

While both pupil size and microsaccades are now known to modulate as a consequence of ongoing attentional activity -thereby providing a rich, complementary measure of visual attention -it is also important to note that they do not offer a complete record of attentional allocation (Smith & Schenk, 2012).
text.formatted: While both pupil size and microsaccades are now known to modulate as a consequence of ongoing attentional activity -thereby providing a rich, complementary measure of visual attention -it is also important to note that they do not offer a complete record of attentional allocation <ref type="bibr" target="#b237">(Smith & Schenk, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Covert attention can be directed to a location without an overt eye movement, as demonstrated by Klink et al. (2023).
text.formatted: Covert attention can be directed to a location without an overt eye movement, as demonstrated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Klink et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: In their study, macaques made saccades directly to a target without ever fixating a salient distractor; yet, neural recordings in V4 revealed a brief, initial attentional enhancement at the distractor location.
This highlights why using the absence of (micro)saccades to infer an absence of attention is problematic: eye movements can fail to reveal transient covert shifts.
Nevertheless, this limitation underscores the value of concurrent eye tracking, particularly alongside EEG.
Though eye-tracking data is already available in many EEG studies, it is frequently underutilized-often relegated solely to artifact control and trial exclusion.
This practice overlooks a valuable, essentially "for free" dataset.

Because covert attention often serves to prepare overt eye movements, integrating these measures allows ocular behavior to constrain the interpretation of neural activity, while neural measures expose the covert dynamics that behavior misses.

Ultimately, a complete account of visual selection requires both; as concurrent recordings become standard practice, the field may well look back on eye-movement integration as a major methodological turning point in the electrophysiological study of attention.
