Duncan, Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld, Clayton Hickey, Anna Schubö, Jan Theeuwes, Dirk van Moorselaar Traditionally, visual attention was best characterized by a dichotomy of two mechanisms: a top-down volitional mechanism defined by the participant's current goals, and a bottom-up automatic system defined by the intrinsic salience of the visual environment (Desimone & Duncan, 1995; Koch & Ullman, 1987; Theeuwes, 2010).
text.formatted: Contributors: Dock H. <ref type="bibr">Duncan, Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld, Clayton Hickey, Anna Schubö, Jan Theeuwes, Dirk van Moorselaar</ref> Traditionally, visual attention was best characterized by a dichotomy of two mechanisms: a top-down volitional mechanism defined by the participant's current goals, and a bottom-up automatic system defined by the intrinsic salience of the visual environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Desimone & Duncan, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Koch & Ullman, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b250">Theeuwes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these modules were thought to capture how attention is guided in a scene.
However, this dichotomy left a critical gap in our understanding of attentional control.
It failed to account for how specific, recent, and incidental experiences dynamically shape ongoing behavior.
Early demonstrations of priming of pop-out showed that recent selection episodes can strongly influence subsequent attentional selection (Maljkovic & Nakayama, 1994 , 1996).
text.formatted: Early demonstrations of priming of pop-out showed that recent selection episodes can strongly influence subsequent attentional selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">(Maljkovic & Nakayama, 1994</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: These findings contributed to a broader realization that attentional control cannot be fully understood in terms of the traditional dichotomy between top-down goals and bottom-up salience.
In an influential paper, Awh et al. (2012) explicitly challenged this prevailing view and argued that, in many instances, attentional selection is shaped by prior selection experiences.
text.formatted: In an influential paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Awh et al. (2012)</ref> explicitly challenged this prevailing view and argued that, in many instances, attentional selection is shaped by prior selection experiences.

text.text: They termed this influence selection history.
According to this view, selection is often not guided solely by the observer's current goals, nor solely by the physical salience of objects in the environment.
Instead, previous encounters with particular features, objects, or locations can bias what is selected on subsequent trials.
Importantly, Awh et al. (2012) argued that effects previously interpreted as evidence for top-down control may, in some cases, be better understood as consequences of selection history.
text.formatted: Importantly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Awh et al. (2012)</ref> argued that effects previously interpreted as evidence for top-down control may, in some cases, be better understood as consequences of selection history.

text.text: This proposal established selection history as a third major component of attentional control, alongside goal-driven and stimulus-driven influences (see also Failing & Theeuwes, 2018; Theeuwes, 2018 Theeuwes, , 2019)), and forms the basis of the recently proposed tripartite model of attention (Theeuwes, 2025).
text.formatted: This proposal established selection history as a third major component of attentional control, alongside goal-driven and stimulus-driven influences (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Failing & Theeuwes, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b251">Theeuwes, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b252">Theeuwes, , 2019))</ref>, and forms the basis of the recently proposed tripartite model of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b253">(Theeuwes, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Since then, the study of selection history has become a central topic in attention research, including the encephalographic study of visual attention.

Considerable ERP work has demonstrated the influence of selection history on the target N2pc and distractor P D -from work on intertrial priming (Eimer et al., 2010; Feldmann-Wüstefeld & Schubö, 2016; Olivers & Hickey, 2010), to associative learning (Do Carmo Blanco & Allen, 2018; Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2015; Qu et al., 2017) and reward learning (Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2016; Hickey et al., 2010 Hickey et al., , 2023;; Kiss et al., 2009; Oemisch et al., 2017; Taylor & Feldmann-Wüstefeld, 2024), abundant work has demonstrated that learning effects are effectively tracked by modulations in amplitude or latency of wellknown attention-related ERPs.
text.formatted: Considerable ERP work has demonstrated the influence of selection history on the target N2pc and distractor P D -from work on intertrial priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Eimer et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Feldmann-Wüstefeld & Schubö, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b203">Olivers & Hickey, 2010)</ref>, to associative learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Do Carmo Blanco & Allen, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b217">Qu et al., 2017)</ref> and reward learning <ref type="bibr">(Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Hickey et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Hickey et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Kiss et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b202">Oemisch et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b248">Taylor & Feldmann-Wüstefeld, 2024)</ref>, abundant work has demonstrated that learning effects are effectively tracked by modulations in amplitude or latency of wellknown attention-related ERPs.

text.text: A key question cutting across these mechanisms is how experience-driven changes influence attentional priority: do they proactively bias processing before the search display appears, or do they operate reactively after a stimulus has been encountered?

Addressing this question requires methods that can reveal the neural mechanisms and temporal dynamics through which recent experience -whether driven by repetition, statistical structure, or learned value -shapes attentional selection.
Central to this new study of learning was the observation that through experience, distracting stimuli can become greatly attenuated.

While the role of top-down control in suppressing distractors is heavily debated (e.g. Addleman & Störmer, 2022; Arita et al., 2012), there is broad agreement that statistical learning offers a robust and efficient mechanism for reducing interference from distracting input.
text.formatted: While the role of top-down control in suppressing distractors is heavily debated (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Addleman & Störmer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Arita et al., 2012)</ref>, there is broad agreement that statistical learning offers a robust and efficient mechanism for reducing interference from distracting input.

text.text: A critical question currently driving M/EEG research is whether this learned suppression operates proactively or reactively (Liesefeld et al., 2024; Luck et al., 2021) -if a region of space receives reduced attentional priority due to learning, is the initial feed-forward sweep of visual information attenuated before it even arrives (proactive)?
text.formatted: A critical question currently driving M/EEG research is whether this learned suppression operates proactively or reactively <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">(Liesefeld et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b169">Luck et al., 2021)</ref> -if a region of space receives reduced attentional priority due to learning, is the initial feed-forward sweep of visual information attenuated before it even arrives (proactive)?

text.text: Or is the information initially selected, only to be rapidly disengaged and suppressed by the attention system (reactive)?
For spatial learning, encephalographic techniques have provided conflicting answers.

Experiments utilizing RIFT, machine learning classification, and novel 'pinging' techniques have revealed shifting spatial attentional priority maps prior to search onset, providing strong neural evidence for a proactive mechanism (D. H. Duncan et al., 2025; Ferrante et al., 2023 Ferrante et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: Experiments utilizing RIFT, machine learning classification, and novel 'pinging' techniques have revealed shifting spatial attentional priority maps prior to search onset, providing strong neural evidence for a proactive mechanism (D. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Duncan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Ferrante et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Ferrante et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: However, other encephalographic studies examining evoked responses to stimuli suggest that even highly suppressed locations may undergo initial selection followed by speeded disengagement (D. H. Duncan et al., 2025; C. Huang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, other encephalographic studies examining evoked responses to stimuli suggest that even highly suppressed locations may undergo initial selection followed by speeded disengagement (D. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Duncan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">C. Huang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Resolving how proactive baseline shifts interact with reactive disengagement mechanisms remains a central debate in the field.
The above section has been primarily concerned with spatial learning of distractor location probabilities.
Feature based suppression is addressed in the following section (feature-based attention).

It is notable, however, that while spatial and feature based learned attention have been extensively and independently studied, it is also known that these two forms of suppression can interact, resulting in feature specific spatial suppression (D. H. Duncan et al., 2024; Failing et al., 2019).
text.formatted: It is notable, however, that while spatial and feature based learned attention have been extensively and independently studied, it is also known that these two forms of suppression can interact, resulting in feature specific spatial suppression (D. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Duncan et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Failing et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the fact that objects in real life often have both feature and spatial regularities (Biederman, 1972), it remains an underexplored question how the interaction of spatial and feature learning bears out in the brain, and whether this combined form of learned suppression reflects both proactive and reactive mechanisms.
text.formatted: Despite the fact that objects in real life often have both feature and spatial regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Biederman, 1972)</ref>, it remains an underexplored question how the interaction of spatial and feature learning bears out in the brain, and whether this combined form of learned suppression reflects both proactive and reactive mechanisms.

text.text: Beyond mapping the temporal dynamics of suppression, determining where and how the brain instantiates these learned changes remains a central, related and unanswered question.
On the one hand, selection history may primarily affect the initial feed-forward sweep of visual processing.

One such feed-forward theory is the synaptic theory of learned attention (D. H. Duncan et al., 2023; Ferrante et al., 2018; van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2020), which proposes that learned spatial suppression arises via alterations in the latent synaptic state of the early visual system -selectively up-and down-weighting spatial locations in the early visual system such that information is passed up the visual processing hierarchy better at expected target location, and worse at expected distractor locations (D. H. Duncan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: One such feed-forward theory is the synaptic theory of learned attention (D. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Duncan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Ferrante et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Moorselaar & Slagter, 2020)</ref>, which proposes that learned spatial suppression arises via alterations in the latent synaptic state of the early visual system -selectively up-and down-weighting spatial locations in the early visual system such that information is passed up the visual processing hierarchy better at expected target location, and worse at expected distractor locations (D. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Duncan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, rather than operating in the early visual cortex, suppression may be expressed subcortically in the hippocampus or basal ganglia -structures more commonly associated with statistical learning and habitual action (Ashby et al., 2010; Schapiro et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Alternatively, rather than operating in the early visual cortex, suppression may be expressed subcortically in the hippocampus or basal ganglia -structures more commonly associated with statistical learning and habitual action <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ashby et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b231">Schapiro et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Such deep structures have been implicated in non-attentional statistical learning tasks, such as sequence learning, navigation or automatic motor learning (Schapiro et al., 2013 (Schapiro et al., , 2017;; Stachenfeld et al., 2017; Yewbrey & Kornysheva, 2024).
text.formatted: Such deep structures have been implicated in non-attentional statistical learning tasks, such as sequence learning, navigation or automatic motor learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b232">(Schapiro et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b233">(Schapiro et al., , 2017;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b240">Stachenfeld et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b291">Yewbrey & Kornysheva, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is thus highly plausible that learned attention bias is coordinated by subcortical regions and fed back to visual areas.
Because standard EEG struggles to definitively localize deep subcortical sources, researchers must push the boundaries of multimodal imaging.
Combining the high temporal resolution of EEG with the spatial precision of fMRI (Mayhew et al., 2013) offers the most promising route to resolving this debate.
text.formatted: Combining the high temporal resolution of EEG with the spatial precision of fMRI <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">(Mayhew et al., 2013)</ref> offers the most promising route to resolving this debate.

text.text: Future research must determine whether learned suppression is mediated by shifting local connectivity that redirects the feed-forward sweep of salience, or if it relies on feedback mechanisms from subcortical structures evaluating the incoming visual volley.

Unlike top-down and bottom-up attention, which are well-described by the biased competition theory (D. M. Beck & Kastner, 2009; Desimone & Duncan, 1995; Reynolds & Heeger, 2009), there is currently no unified neural theory for selection history.
text.formatted: Unlike top-down and bottom-up attention, which are well-described by the biased competition theory (D. M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Beck & Kastner, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Desimone & Duncan, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b221">Reynolds & Heeger, 2009)</ref>, there is currently no unified neural theory for selection history.

text.text: This presents a clear knowledge gap to be filled in the literature: understanding the neural characterization of selection history to match that of top-down and bottom-up attention.

This section has highlighted two topics of special interest in the field currently; identifying learned attentional bias as proactive versus reactive in nature, and whether this bias originates in structural changes in subcortical learning systems or in the visual cortex itself -thus reflecting feedforward or feedback mechanisms in the brain.
Importantly, these two questions are highly interrelated as a feed-forward mechanism is in principle more compatible with a proactive mechanism than a feedback mechanism.

And conversely, a feed-back mechanism originating from subcortical regions (such as the thalamus or pulvinar) and exerting control back onto the early visual system is conceptually aligned with a reactive disengagement system.

Thus, understanding how experience changes the neural priority map is essential for determining whether learning biases attention proactively, before the search display appears, or reactively, after the display has been encountered.

More broadly, this question echoes the argument made by Awh et al. (2012), who showed that the traditional dichotomy between top-down and bottom-up control is insufficient to explain the full range of attentional behavior.
text.formatted: More broadly, this question echoes the argument made by <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Awh et al. (2012)</ref>, who showed that the traditional dichotomy between top-down and bottom-up control is insufficient to explain the full range of attentional behavior.

text.text: In much the same way, current neural models of attention remain incomplete if they do not adequately incorporate selection history.

Further research is therefore needed to bring neural accounts of attention in line with what is now widely accepted at the behavioral level: that prior selection experiences play a central role in shaping attentional priority.

For decades, research has consistently implicated non-spatial feature space-such as color or motion direction-as a critical guide for attention (Anllo-Vento & Hillyard, 1996; Hillyard & Anllo-Vento, 1998; Hillyard & Münte, 1984; M. Müller et al., 2006; Treue & Trujillo, 1999).

text.text: Based on seminal animal studies, Treue and colleagues suggested the feature similarity gain model (Treue, 2001; Treue & Trujillo, 1999), proposing that attentional selection of a feature facilitates all stimuli sharing the same feature throughout the visual field (global feature upweighting).

text.text: A key paradigm is to present spatially superimposed Random Dot Kinematograms (RDKs), each having a different color and flickering at different frequencies.
Human observers were instructed to shift attention to one of the RDKs and to respond to target events in the to-be-attended while ignoring such events in the to-be-ignored color.
The typical finding is that attending a feature led to greater SSVEP power throughout the display than when not attending it (M. Müller et al., 2006).

text.text: While the basic mechanisms of feature-based attention are now wellestablished, their generalization to visual search is a central focus of the field today.

Particularly, there are twofoot_1 open questions in regard to the efficiency of search based on feature subsets (known as subset selective search whereby humans efficiently select certain sets of colors to restrict their search; Egeth et al., 1984; Kaptein et al., 1995): whether multiple features can be simultaneously upweighted, leading to multiple template search, and whether global facilitation can be inverted to suppress certain color features, especially when these features come in the form of salient singletons.
text.formatted: Particularly, there are two<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> open questions in regard to the efficiency of search based on feature subsets (known as subset selective search whereby humans efficiently select certain sets of colors to restrict their search; <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Egeth et al., 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Kaptein et al., 1995)</ref>: whether multiple features can be simultaneously upweighted, leading to multiple template search, and whether global facilitation can be inverted to suppress certain color features, especially when these features come in the form of salient singletons.

text.text: Both of these questions involve the concept of an attentional template -a putative memory representation consisting of target related features that guides attention.
Both of these questions seek to elucidate features of these putative templates; asking in turn whether they can be multiplied into multiple-template search, or inverted into negative templates.

Directing attention towards a certain feature requires activation of an internal representation of that feature in visual working memory, often referred to as an attentional template (Carlisle et al., 2011; J. Duncan & Humphreys, 1992; Eimer, 2014; Olivers et al., 2011; Soto et al., 2008).

text.text: Influential early accounts proposed that attentional guidance is restricted to a single active template at a time (Dombrowe et al., 2011; Houtkamp & Roelfsema, 2009; Olivers et al., 2011).

text.text: Given that visual working memory can typically maintain three to four representations (Cowan, 2001), this would mean that the attention-guiding capacity is functionally dissociated from maintenance capacity.

text.text: Consequently, research has shifted toward understanding two fundamental questions: (i) at which stage observable capacity limitations emerge, and (ii) what determines the effective capacity of multiple-template search.
The first unresolved question concerns the stage at which capacity limitations arise.

Frequency-tagging studies point to a high capacity for parallel processing, showing simultaneous enhancement for multiple attended colors (S. K. Andersen et al., 2013; Martinovic et al., 2018) and additive modulation across features (S. K. Andersen et al., 2008), suggesting no selection bottleneck before search begins.

text.text: Other electrophysiological studies observe N2pc reductions and delays when multiple search templates are maintained, suggesting mutual inhibition between templates rather than serial processing (Grubert et al., 2016 (Grubert et al., , 2025;; Grubert & Eimer, 2015 , 2016; Jimenez et al., 2024; Z. text.text: Rapid Serial Probe Presentation (RSPP) paradigms confirm this by showing that N2pc responses to target-color probes reflecting preparatory template activation, were virtually identical during single-and two-color search (Grubert & Eimer, 2020 , 2023), demonstrating that costs do not originate from template preparation (Dodwell et al., 2026; Grubert & Eimer, 2018).

text.text: However, behavioral costs do emerge after the search display appears, during target selection itself.

Evidence from multivariate decoding indicates that while observers can prepare for two colors, attention struggles to access both these colors simultaneously in a display; once a matching stimulus triggers one feature set, it automatically inhibits the other, imposing a serial bottleneck during actual selection of the stimulus (Ort et al., 2019; c.f. L. Huang & Pashler, 2007).

text.text: If multiple templates can activate concurrently, the next question is what determines their effective capacity.

Firstly, it's important to note that measuring the upper limits of template activation is complicated by methodological issues like trial averaging (Ort & Olivers, 2020) which can make it seem like multiple templates are maintained even if on a trial-by-trial basis only one item actually is.

text.text: Second, different tasks may invoke different strategies, and observers may not always activate multiple templates even if they can.

For example when observers can freely choose between two targets, observers exhibit signs of proactive control as indicated by (pre-trial betaband suppression in the EEG) with little performance costs, whereas when different targets are externally imposed, switches costs arise along with signatures of reactive control (via enhanced delta/theta signals suggesting a wait-and-see approach; van Driel et al., 2019).

text.text: Additionally, if there is a temporal order for which template will be used in the upcoming trial structure, participants will simply strategically activate only the immediately relevant template to reduce memory load (Grubert et al., 2025; Grubert & Eimer, 2020).

text.text: Because active templates mutually inhibit one another, adding templates progressively reduces individual activation strength (Kerzel & Grubert, 2022; Ort et al., 2019).

text.text: This causes parallel guidance to become increasingly inefficient as more templates are added, eventually making serial switching a more effective search strategy.
Taken together, current evidence suggests that the capacity to prepare multiple feature representations substantially exceeds the capacity to use them efficiently during target selection.

Future research must dissociate preparatory feature activation from target selection to determine whether search limits reflect a fixed capacity constraint or emerge gradually from competitive, inhibitory interactions between active representations.
Can global feature upweighting be inverted, suppressing the evoked activity of certain features?
The influential signal suppression hypothesis is largely a feature-based account of suppression.

At its core is the assumption that specific feature signals can be proactively downregulated, in much the same way that feature-based attention can selectively upweight relevant color signals (Gaspelin et al., 2025, see the section on the role of learning in suppression for additional discussion).

text.text: Recent work has shown that the global upweighting of expected target features is a proactive process, spreading to unattended areas of the screen prior to search target onset (Menceloglu et al., 2026).

text.text: Signal suppression therefore proposes a reversal of this global upweighting, an inversion of this mechanism to proactively suppress certain feature signals before any visual input has been processed, thereby preventing their intrusion on attentional processing (Gaspelin et al., 2015; Gaspelin & Luck, 2018b).

text.text: Importantly, unlike feature guided search which can be dynamically altered on a trial-by-trial basis (and thus implicates working memory as a core function), signal suppression cannot enact itself on a trial-by-trial basis (Addleman & Störmer, 2022; Cunningham & Egeth, 2016; Moher & Egeth, 2012), but instead requires some amount of experience before suppression can kick in (Gaspelin et al., 2019; Savelson et al., 2025; Y. Zhang & Gaspelin, 2026).

Zhang & Gaspelin, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This has led proponents of signal suppression to rebrand the mechanism as a form of selection history (Gaspelin et al., 2025), relying more on long term memory and casting doubt on the proposal that signal suppression is an exact inversion of the well-established global upweighting effect.

text.text: Alternatively, it has been proposed that signal suppression may not reflect suppression at all but instead is simply the enhancement of features known to belong to the search target but not the distractor (such as color).
The enhancement of expected target color may then masquerade as suppression if care is not taken in the experimental design.

Oxner and colleagues (Oxner et al., 2023; Oxner, Forschack, et al., 2024) demonstrated that much of the feature suppression effect can in fact be accounted for by enhancement of the known expected target color -as evident by the abolition of probe suppression effects when target colors varied randomly rather than being fixed as is commonly done in paradigms studying signal suppression.

text.text: This sequential account, in which attentional capture precedes rather than is prevented by suppression, finds neural support from feature-cuing designs.

Temporal neural dynamics of color directed attention shifts revealed that facilitation of the target color and suppression of the tobe-ignored color do not operate on the same timescale, but instead exhibit a bi-phasic process, in which fast facilitation is followed by a temporally delayed suppression (S. Andersen & Müller, 2010; Gundlach et al., 2022 Gundlach et al., , 2023)).

text.text: It remains a topic of debate whether feature suppression truly represents suppression rather than enhancement of target guided features, and further whether this modulation can truly be characterized as proactive rather than reactive (Liesefeld et al., 2024).

text.text: Notably, the above research has heavily focused on the role of color-based suppression in the visual system.

This is due to the ease in which color manipulations are implemented in experimental paradigms, as well as the color-centric nature of the human visual system (with color information already present in the earliest phases of visual processing in the retina).
Despite this, some work has highlighted that suppression may occur also for other feature dimensions, including shape (Kim et al., 2023) and motion (Adams & Gaspelin, 2024).

text.text: Notably, recent work comparing color to motion distractors has observed clearly distinct neural patterns relating to each format of distractor (van Moorselaar et al., 2025), raising crucial questions about the generality of neural responses measured in studies often focused on color-based distractors.

text.text: This calls for future work to investigate whether suppression of divergent features is handled by a single mechanism applied differentially across feature maps, or whether perhaps completely separate cognitive mechanisms exist for different feature dimensions.

The study of nonspatial attention remains an active and vital area of research, particularly regarding how the brain weights feature subsets to direct attention toward task-relevant characteristics and away from distracting ones.

A central challenge within this domain is determining whether feature-based suppression exists as an independent cognitive mechanism-operating via the proactive or reactive downregulation of unwanted signals-or whether it simply reflects a relative change in priority driven by the selective enhancement of all other competing features.
This debate is closely tied to the architectural constraints of working memory.

While it is well established that humans can hold multiple items in working memory simultaneously (Luck & Vogel, 1997), it remains a mystery why guiding attention via multiple target templates is so difficult to observe, and whether negative templates can actively suppress distracting features rather than merely upweighting competing ones.
text.formatted: While it is well established that humans can hold multiple items in working memory simultaneously <ref type="bibr" target="#b174">(Luck & Vogel, 1997)</ref>, it remains a mystery why guiding attention via multiple target templates is so difficult to observe, and whether negative templates can actively suppress distracting features rather than merely upweighting competing ones.

text.text: Resolving these questions and identifying the cognitive bottlenecks that limit the concurrent use of multiple templates remains critical for a complete account of nonspatial attentional selection.

text.text: Rather than being driven solely by incoming stimulation, observers continuously regulate what information is encountered in the first place.

For example, eye movements can be directed away from distracting or irrelevant stimuli to attenuate their sensory consequences (Abeles & Yuval-Greenberg, 2021), and gaze trajectories themselves reflect strategic avoidance of known distractor locations (Van der Stigchel & Theeuwes, 2006).

text.text: Moreover, visual selection in the real world is tightly coupled to overt action.
Searching for an object in real life often involves coordinated eye, head, and body movements, as well as manual interactions such as reaching, grasping, or repositioning items.

These actions do not merely select relevant information, they also actively exclude alternative sources of input by determining what is fixated, approached, or manipulated, and what is left uninspected.

As a result, attentional selection in natural environments is inherently embodied and sequential, unfolding through cycles of sampling and action that are largely absent from traditional, fixation-based, "sit-in-front-of-a-computer" paradigms.
This creates an important gap between laboratory models of attentional selection and the active sampling that characterizes natural vision.

While classic paradigms have been undeniably instrumental in uncovering the core neural mechanisms of attention, a persistent question is to what degree findings in these highly controlled environments reflect attentional processing in the real world.

It is possible that the reliance on artificial stimuli and setups leaves core attentional mechanisms opaque which would be apparent if attention was studied in more realworld environments using naturalistic stimuli.

Already, research has shown that naturalistic stimuli are processed differently from artificial stimuli, both when examining behavior (Biederman, 1972; Li et al., 2002) and neural processing (S. V. David et al., 2004; Kisker et al., 2025; Marini et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Already, research has shown that naturalistic stimuli are processed differently from artificial stimuli, both when examining behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Biederman, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">Li et al., 2002)</ref> and neural processing (S. V. <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">David et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Kisker et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">Marini et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This serves as ever-present motivation for fundamental vision researchers to expand their research to use naturalistic stimuli to observe how neural responses differ from viewing synthetic stimuli and potentially unlock new layers of neural processing that would be otherwise obscured.

Luckily, the research program to study the neural correlates of natural vision has been buoyed by the many recent advances in techniques and technology that has allowed researchers to confidently interpret patterns of brain activity while participants make free eye movements and attend to real world objects (Dimigen, 2020; Fakche et al., 2024; Sulewski et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Luckily, the research program to study the neural correlates of natural vision has been buoyed by the many recent advances in techniques and technology that has allowed researchers to confidently interpret patterns of brain activity while participants make free eye movements and attend to real world objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Dimigen, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Fakche et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b244">Sulewski et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While in principle, attention research using real-world stimuli can still occur in the experimental cubicle, perhaps the greatest driver of attentional research in real-world search is technical advances in mobile EEG (mEEG) allowing researchers to move away from the chinrest and observe attentional processing live in the real (or virtual) world.

Because the ultimate goal of attention research is to understand and predict when and where people attend in the real world, advances made possible by combining mEEG with eye tracking provide an important bridge between fundamental research on attention and its application to naturalistic environments.
These novel frontiers also encourage new research questions that differ from their more traditional, laboratorybound counterparts.
In controlled lab tasks, often stimuli are presented in a truly random configuration from trial to trial.

This does not reflect the structure of the real world, where patterns govern the placement of things such that visual attention is often aided by a rich history of experience which helps to guide attention in an optimal pattern.

This intrinsic statistical structure has been the subject of great research interest in the past decade in the form of selection history effects in synthetic displays (B. A. Anderson et al., 2021; Theeuwes et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This intrinsic statistical structure has been the subject of great research interest in the past decade in the form of selection history effects in synthetic displays (B. A. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Anderson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b254">Theeuwes et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: By embedding patterns in a search task, participants effectively and automatically encode these patterns to improve search performance.
But real-world regularities that guide search are far more complicated than the simple caricature presented in most visual statistical learning studies.

Often these regularities are not so simple as a retinotopic high probability location that persists for several minutes, but instead are intricate patterns of embedded knowledge that guides search in a structure akin to the structure of language (Biederman, 1976).
text.formatted: Often these regularities are not so simple as a retinotopic high probability location that persists for several minutes, but instead are intricate patterns of embedded knowledge that guides search in a structure akin to the structure of language <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Biederman, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: The "scene grammar" framework (Draschkow & Vo, 2017; Võ, 2021; Võ et al., 2019) captures how attention is guided in everyday life by patterns learned through a lifetime of experience.
text.formatted: The "scene grammar" framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Draschkow & Vo, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b273">Võ, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b274">Võ et al., 2019)</ref> captures how attention is guided in everyday life by patterns learned through a lifetime of experience.

text.text: For instance, when searching for a toothbrush in a bathroom one may automatically retrieve the knowledge that toothbrushes are often found on top of the sink and automatically direct their search towards this visible "anchor".
According to this framework, scenes are structured hierarchically in that a scene can be decomposed in meaningful, functionally optimized clusters of objects known as "phrases."
At the heart of these phrases, anchors predict not only the identity but also the location of other local objects.

Scene grammar therefore allows the human attention system to ignore vast swaths of a visual scene (such as a shower or toilet "phrase" when looking for a toothbrush) and limit the search space strictly to the relevant anchor and its phrase (Kaiser et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Scene grammar therefore allows the human attention system to ignore vast swaths of a visual scene (such as a shower or toilet "phrase" when looking for a toothbrush) and limit the search space strictly to the relevant anchor and its phrase <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">(Kaiser et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This top-down conceptualization of attention moves away from the feed forward sweep of attention that has often been the subject of study in artificial stimuli to more complex multistep search which better characterizes attentional guidance in real life.

Naturalistic search is often said to comprise of selective and non-selective processing pathways, meant to capture how attention is guided by scene gist knowledge retrieved from episodic memory and unrelated to actual current features of the visual scene, that guide selective attention (J. M. Wolfe et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Naturalistic search is often said to comprise of selective and non-selective processing pathways, meant to capture how attention is guided by scene gist knowledge retrieved from episodic memory and unrelated to actual current features of the visual scene, that guide selective attention (J. M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b285">Wolfe et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Extant work has robustly established the N400 as a marker of violations of scene grammar rules (Draschkow et al., 2018; Nicholls et al., 2025; Võ & Wolfe, 2013; for a review, see Lauer & Võ, 2022), reliably capturing violations in this nonselective pathway.
text.formatted: Extant work has robustly established the N400 as a marker of violations of scene grammar rules <ref type="bibr">(Draschkow et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nicholls et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Võ & Wolfe, 2013</ref>; for a review, see Lauer & Võ, 2022), reliably capturing violations in this nonselective pathway.

text.text: Furthermore, the P D ERP, a marker of suppression, effectively captures how gist guidance affects the very early guidance of visual search, constraining the search space before target presence can be processed (Hickey et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the P D ERP, a marker of suppression, effectively captures how gist guidance affects the very early guidance of visual search, constraining the search space before target presence can be processed <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">(Hickey et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, the deeper question of how these rules are stored and accessed dynamically to guide visual search mere milliseconds after the first feedforward sweep of attention remains considerably underexplored.
Thus, the use of scene grammar during visual search reflects an interplay between perception, memory, and attention that is still poorly understood.

Utilizing mEEG in combination with eye tracking as well as multivariate analyses may provide a powerful way to examine how learned regularities are retrieved and implemented during naturalistic search, allowing researchers to track both where observers look and how the brain prepares, guides, and updates attentional priorities in real time.

It is commonly presumed that feature guided search involves the loading of a feature template into working memory, with subsequent search essentially being the serial loading and comparing of visual percepts against this putative template.

This is often reflected by canonical search tasks where a certain synthetic stimulus is presented as the search target and participants know with 100% certainty how this item will look in the upcoming search trials (J. M. Wolfe, 1994; J. M. Wolfe et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This is often reflected by canonical search tasks where a certain synthetic stimulus is presented as the search target and participants know with 100% certainty how this item will look in the upcoming search trials (J. M. Wolfe, 1994; J. M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b285">Wolfe et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to this, objects in the real world differ in at least two major dimensions -firstly their presentation varies considerably such that a coffee mug can appear in any myriad of shapes depending on the angle from which it is viewed, and various retinal sizes depending on whether it is located nearby or far away.

Despite this template variability, attentional guidance towards 'mugs' is quite efficient, showing resilience to perceptual variability and a seeming awareness of a three-dimensional structure underlying the two-dimensional percept (Yu et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Despite this template variability, attentional guidance towards 'mugs' is quite efficient, showing resilience to perceptual variability and a seeming awareness of a three-dimensional structure underlying the two-dimensional percept <ref type="bibr" target="#b292">(Yu et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This reflects a form of categorical search (where the participant is given a vague search template rather than the exact visual appearance of the upcoming search target; Castelhano et al., 2008; Yang & Zelinsky, 2009) and broadly speaking, this approach better approximates the ambiguity inherent in real world object search.
text.formatted: This reflects a form of categorical search (where the participant is given a vague search template rather than the exact visual appearance of the upcoming search target; <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Castelhano et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b290">Yang & Zelinsky, 2009)</ref> and broadly speaking, this approach better approximates the ambiguity inherent in real world object search.

text.text: Secondly, real-world objects are often searched for with explicit goals for interaction.

This means that the affordances of an object are particularly important during viewing, because visual information is not collected merely for identification, but also to guide subsequent motor interactions with the object.

Recent behavioral and fMRI work suggests that search templates for real-world objects in naturalistic scenes are highly dynamic, and may simultaneously combine context-dependent features (e.g., adjusting expected size based on viewing distance) with context-invariant features that may generalize across searches, such as object orientation (Gayet et al., 2024; Gayet & Peelen, 2022; Lerebourg et al., 2026; Reeder & Peelen, 2013) or action plans (Trentin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent behavioral and fMRI work suggests that search templates for real-world objects in naturalistic scenes are highly dynamic, and may simultaneously combine context-dependent features (e.g., adjusting expected size based on viewing distance) with context-invariant features that may generalize across searches, such as object orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(Gayet et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Gayet & Peelen, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Lerebourg et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b220">Reeder & Peelen, 2013)</ref> or action plans <ref type="bibr" target="#b257">(Trentin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A crucial open question for M/EEG research is how these multiple representational levels operate temporally.

Future work aims to leverage M/EEG in combination with Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) to track, in real time, the evolving representational content of these search templates during preparation and detection, uncovering how the brain juggles abstraction and specificity on the fly.

Furthermore, an often-underappreciated feature of visual search in the real world is that the current target of search is often not actually present in sight, but the larger act of 'searching' often requires several steps to locate the current goal targets.

For instance, searching for a spoon may guide attention to a spoon on a counter, or otherwise it may guide attention towards a drawer which needs to be pulled open and only then will reveal a set of silverware.
These multi-step searches that integrate motor demands are ubiquitous in everyday life, and describes a format of search that is nearly never studied in experimental settings (E. David & Vo, 2022).
text.formatted: These multi-step searches that integrate motor demands are ubiquitous in everyday life, and describes a format of search that is nearly never studied in experimental settings (E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">David & Vo, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Paradigms utilizing VR setups have proven especially promising in this regard, as attention is connected to behavior in more complex investigations into decision making (Duarte & Geng, 2024).
text.formatted: Paradigms utilizing VR setups have proven especially promising in this regard, as attention is connected to behavior in more complex investigations into decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Duarte & Geng, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Leveraging recent developments in mEEG along with multivariate approaches able to separate neural processes from noisy data promises to offer new avenues for studying the complex relationship between attention and decision making in such complex tasks.
Such research programs promise to better capture the role attention plays in everyday life.
Basic research into the mechanisms underlying attentional selection has generated important theories that help explain search behavior.

Much of this work has relied on simplified stimuli and two-dimensional displays, allowing researchers to isolate core mechanisms under tightly controlled conditions that do not permit active movement.

It is now increasingly possible to test these theories in more naturalistic settings, for example by examining the neural correlates of attention while participants view, search, and act within virtual or augmented reality environments.
Pivoting toward more naturalistic stimuli inevitably requires researchers to confront the increased variability and noise that such settings introduce.
Fortunately, methodological advances have made it increasingly possible to extract meaningful information from these richer but noisier data.
Particularly important are recent developments in multivariate analysis techniques (the increased use of representational similarity analysis with EEG).

These developing approaches allow researchers to move beyond traditional, often noisy, ERP components by decomposing the EEG response into increasingly refined underlying (theoretical) representations and further to relate these multivariate responses to the activations of artificial vision models (e.g., convolutional neural networks).
In parallel, advances in linear mixedeffects modeling have improved the interpretability of complex data by better accounting for variability across participants, stimuli, trials, and contexts.

Although Hans Berger is widely regarded as the founding father of EEG recording following his first report of the human electroencephalogram in 1929 (İnce et al., 2021; Mushtaq et al., 2024), the systematic use of EEG to study visual attention began several decades later.
text.formatted: Although Hans Berger is widely regarded as the founding father of EEG recording following his first report of the human electroencephalogram in 1929 <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">(İnce et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b200">Mushtaq et al., 2024)</ref>, the systematic use of EEG to study visual attention began several decades later.

text.text: Building on earlier work by Robert Eason and colleagues (1969), Steven Hillyard and colleagues demonstrated and popularized the method of measuring EEG to observe how attention modulates visual processing in the human brain (Luck & Hillyard, 1994a , 1994b; G. R. Mangun & Hillyard, 1991; Van Voorhis & Hillyard, 1977).

R. Mangun & Hillyard, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b270">Van Voorhis & Hillyard, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: Since then, the study of electrical brain activity in relation to visual attention has become a lively and highly productive field of research.

Over the past 55 years, electroencephalographic methods have provided a unique window into the neural mechanisms of visual attention, revealing patterns of brain activity that would have been difficult, if not impossible, to observe without a temporally precise measure of neural processing.

The international symposium "Advances in the Encephalographic Study of Attention" held in the summer of 2025 provided a snapshot into some of the topics and techniques that may come to define the coming decades of attention research using electro-and magneto-encephalographic measurements.

Exciting technical advances were paired with theoretical developments all highlighting persistent mysteries of the human attention system and how researchers hope to expand our knowledge of it in the future.
Moving forward, the future of M/EEG research continues to be promising as the preferred technique for capturing the brain dynamics that underlie the rapid mechanisms of visual attention.
